13526: Romans: God's Faithfulness, One Family, and the Good News of Jesus as Lord
13527:
Romans is Paul's longest letter and the one that has shaped Christian theology more than almost any other book. Augustine was converted reading Romans 13. Luther found his breakthrough in Romans 1:17. John Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' hearing Luther's preface to Romans read aloud. Many evangelicals learned the gospel through the 'Romans Road' (a short chain of verses from Romans used in evangelism).

But Romans was first a real letter, carried by a real woman (Phoebe) to a handful of house churches in the capital of the empire around AD 57. Paul had never been there. The believers were a mix of Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles) who did not always eat at the same table or keep the same holy days. Paul wanted their support for a mission to Spain, and he was about to take a money gift from Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem.

This study reads Romans chapter by chapter through that first setting: Israel's covenant story (God's binding promise-relationship with Abraham's family), Torah as God's gift, the hope that God would end Israel's exile and bless the nations, and a Roman world of honour and shame, patrons and clients, and an emperor hailed as 'son of god' whose reign was called 'good news' and 'peace'. It also sets out, fairly, where scholars disagree about Romans and why it matters.
13528: Read Romans as a letter about the faithfulness of Israel's God. God promised Abraham a worldwide family and promised to put the world right. Paul argues that in the death and resurrection of Jesus, Israel's Messiah (anointed king), God has kept those promises: he has dealt with sin, made one family out of Jews and Gentiles, given the Spirit, and not abandoned Israel. Salvation is deeply personal, but in Romans it is never only private. It is about being brought into a people, under a new Lord, living in a new way together.
13529: God's righteousness is God's covenant faithfulness
13530: In the Hebrew Bible, God's 'righteousness' (tsedaqah) often means God acting rightly and faithfully to rescue his people and keep his promises. Paul opens and builds his argument on this idea. Scholars debate how much it also means a status God gives to people; most now agree it includes God's own saving action, not only a gift handed over.
13531: Abraham's family is the question behind the questions
13532: Who belongs to Abraham's family, and on what basis? Paul answers: all who share Abraham's trust in the God who raises the dead, whether circumcised or not. Romans 4 is not a side illustration; it is the hinge of the argument.
13533: Israel's story: Adam, exile and return
13534: Paul reads human history through Adam's fall and Israel's history through sin, exile and the promise of return. Jesus is the faithful one who undoes Adam's disobedience and brings the long-awaited 'return' of God's presence by the Spirit.
13535: Torah is holy, but it cannot give life by itself
13536: Paul never calls the Law evil. It is holy, just and good, a gift of the covenant. The problem is sin using the Law, and human flesh that cannot keep it. Paul also resists making the Law a badge that keeps Gentiles out.
13537: Grace as a gift that creates a relationship
13538: In the Roman world, a gift (charis) bound giver and receiver together; the receiver owed gratitude and loyalty. John Barclay shows that Paul's radical point is that God gives to the unworthy, without regard to prior worth, yet the gift still expects a transformed life in return.
13540: The Greek word pistis covers belief, trust, faithfulness and loyalty. Paul speaks of the 'obedience of faith' among the nations, framing the letter. Matthew Bates argues this includes allegiance to Jesus as king; others stress that faith is receiving, not achieving.
13542: Roman inscriptions called the emperor's birth 'good news' (euangelion), Augustus 'son of a god', and the empire's order 'peace'. Paul's gospel announces another Son of God, risen from the dead, whose peace comes through reconciliation. Scholars debate how deliberate the contrast is.
13543: One table: a letter for a divided church
13544: Romans ends with practical appeals: welcome one another as Christ welcomed you. Many scholars think chapters 14-15, about food and days, show what the whole argument is driving at: Jews and Gentiles glorifying God with one voice.
13546: Do we need to become Jews (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath) to be full members? Has God finished with Israel now that so many Jews do not believe? Some were tempted to look down on Jewish believers and their scruples (Rom 11:18-20).
13547: Jewish believers (including returnees after Claudius's expulsion)
13548: Is God still faithful to Israel? Is the Torah being thrown away? Why are uncircumcised Gentiles treated as equals? Some returned from exile under Claudius to find Gentile-led house churches with different habits.
13549: Paul's friends and co-workers named in chapter 16
13550: Prisca and Aquila, Junia and Andronicus and others who knew Paul. They could vouch for him and help the churches receive his letter and his Spain mission.
13551: Household slaves, freedpeople and the poor
13552: Many names in Romans 16 are typical slave or freed names. For them, talk of slavery to sin, redemption, adoption and being heirs would land with special force. (Overlaps with the groups above; share is rough.)
13554: Paul introduces himself and the gospel about David's descendant, declared Son of God by resurrection. The gospel is God's power to save the Jew first and also the Greek, because God's righteousness is revealed in it.
13555: All have sinned: Gentile and Jew
13556: Gentile idolatry leads to disorder; Jews who judge others do the same things. Having the Law does not exempt anyone. The whole world is accountable to God.
13558: Now, apart from the Law, God's righteousness is revealed through the faith(fulness) of Jesus the Messiah, whose death is the place of atonement. God is shown to be just and the one who justifies.
13559: Abraham, father of all who trust
13560: Abraham was counted righteous by trust before circumcision, so he is father of believing Jews and Gentiles alike. God's promise was always to give him many nations.
13561: Peace with God; Adam and Christ
13562: Justified, we have peace and hope. Christ's obedience overturns Adam's disobedience; where sin multiplied, grace multiplied more.
13563: Dead to sin, alive to God
13564: Grace is not licence. Baptised into Christ's death and resurrection, believers change masters: from slavery to sin to slavery to God.
13565: The Law is good, sin is the problem
13566: Believers have died to the Law's rule. The Law is holy, but sin hijacked it; the 'I' who delights in the Law cannot do what it commands. Who will rescue me?
13567: Life in the Spirit; new creation
13568: No condemnation for those in Christ. The Spirit fulfils the Law's just requirement in us, makes us God's children and heirs, and points to the renewal of all creation. Nothing can separate us from God's love.
13570: If nothing can separate us from God's love, what about Israel? God's promise has always worked by calling and mercy, through a remnant, and now includes Gentiles.
13571: The word is near: confess Jesus as Lord
13572: Christ is the goal of the Law. Deuteronomy's 'word near you' is now the message of faith. Anyone, Jew or Greek, who calls on the Lord will be saved, so messengers must be sent.
13574: God has not rejected his people. Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree and must not boast. Israel's stumbling is temporary; God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. Doxology.
13576: In view of God's mercies, believers offer their bodies as living worship, use their gifts in one body, love enemies, live wisely under rulers, and love their neighbour as the fulfilling of the Law.
13577: Welcome one another: strong and weak
13578: Do not despise or judge one another over food and days. Christ became a servant to the circumcised for God's truthfulness and so that the nations might glorify God. Paul's plans: Jerusalem, Rome, Spain.
13580: Phoebe is commended; some 26 people and several households are greeted, Jews and Gentiles, women and men, slaves and free. A final warning against division and a doxology to the God who strengthens through the gospel.
13581: The Gospel of God's Son and a World Gone Wrong
13582: Paul introduces himself as a slave of the Messiah and an apostle sent to bring about 'the obedience of faith' among all nations. His gospel is about God's Son, descended from David and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection. He states his theme: the gospel is God's power for salvation to the Jew first and also the Greek, because in it God's righteousness is revealed. Then he describes how humanity exchanged the glory of God for idols, and how God 'handed them over' to the consequences.
13583: Paul writes from Corinth around AD 57, near the end of his third journey (Acts 20:2-3). He has never visited Rome, though he has long wanted to (Rom 1:13). The Roman believers met in several house churches. Jewish believers had been expelled from Rome under Emperor Claudius around AD 49 (the Roman historian Suetonius says Jews were expelled for disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus', probably a garbled reference to Christ; compare Acts 18:2). After Claudius died in AD 54 many returned, to find churches now led largely by Gentiles. Paul writes partly to introduce his gospel, partly to gain support for a mission to Spain.
13584: Paul's opening reads like a royal announcement. In the Roman world, 'gospel' (euangelion) was used for good news of an emperor's birth, accession or victory; Augustus was called divi filius, 'son of the divine (Julius)'. Paul announces a different Son of God, enthroned not by a senate vote but by resurrection. 'Slave' (doulos) was a real social category; a slave of a powerful household carried its master's authority. Honour and shame drive verses 18-32: humans refused to give God the honour (doxa, glory) due to him, and their own lives became dishonoured. 'I am not ashamed of the gospel' is a bold claim in a culture where a crucified Lord was the height of shame.
13585: Paul's gospel was 'promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures' (1:2): it is the next chapter of Israel's story, not a new religion. Jesus is the 'seed of David', the promised king of 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 2. 'The righteous shall live by faith' quotes Habakkuk 2:4, written when Babylon threatened Judah and the faithful had to trust God's promise. The description of idolatry in 1:18-32 echoes Jewish critiques like the Wisdom of Solomon 13-14 and Israel's own story: 'they exchanged their glory' recalls the golden calf (Ps 106:20) and Jeremiah 2:11. Paul uses a Jewish argument everyone would cheer, then turns it in chapter 2.
13586: Gentile believers would recognise their own past in the description of idols and the moral chaos that followed. Jewish believers would hear a familiar synagogue sermon against pagan idolatry and nod along. Both would notice the ordering 'to the Jew first' (1:16): Gentiles are reminded that the gospel came through Israel, while Jews are reminded that it is also for the Greek.
13587: Romans 1 is often used only for its list of sins. Its deeper point is that every human disorder grows from failing to honour and thank God (1:21). It also challenges every nationalism and every 'Caesar' by naming Jesus, the risen Davidic king, as the true Son of God. Readers should remember the chapter is a set-up: Paul is about to say that those who judge others are no better off.
13588: 'The righteous shall live by faith(fulness)': in Habakkuk, trusting God's promise while the empire rages. Paul makes it the theme verse of Romans.
13589: God promises David a descendant whose kingdom will last and who will be God's son. Rom 1:3-4 announces its fulfilment.
13590: 'You are my son, today I have begotten you': the royal enthronement psalm behind 'declared Son of God in power'.
13591: Israel 'exchanged their glory' for an image of an ox at Sinai; Rom 1:23 uses the same language, so even the anti-pagan charge has Israel's story in it.
13592: The Lord has revealed his righteousness and remembered his faithfulness to Israel in the sight of the nations.
13593: Romans 1:18-32 is mainly a list proving how wicked 'they' (pagans, or today's culture) are.
13594: Paul uses a standard Jewish critique of Gentile sin to set up a trap: in 2:1 he turns to anyone who agrees and says 'you who judge do the same things'. The passage shows that all humanity, including the judge, needs God's rescue.
13595: No Favouritism: Judgment for the Judge
13596: Paul turns on the reader who condemns pagan sin: you do the same things. God judges impartially, according to what each person has done, Jew and Gentile alike. Having the Law and circumcision is a gift, but it does not protect anyone who breaks it. True Jewishness is a matter of the heart, circumcised by the Spirit.
13597: In Rome, Jewish communities were well established, with several synagogues, and some Gentiles had been attracted to them as 'God-fearers'. Paul addresses an imagined conversation partner, first anyone who judges (2:1), then one who 'calls himself a Jew' (2:17). Scholars debate whether this second figure is a Jewish teacher, or (as Rafael Rodríguez and Runar Thorsteinsson argue) a Gentile who has taken on Jewish identity and now judges others.
13598: Paul uses a teaching style called diatribe: an imagined dialogue with a conversation partner, common in Stoic philosophers like Epictetus. Readers should hear it as lively argument, not a personal attack. 'God shows no partiality' (prosōpolēmpsia, literally 'receiving the face') hits a society where courts openly favoured the honourable and wealthy. Honour language continues: 'glory, honour and immortality' versus 'wrath and fury'.
13599: Paul draws on Israel's own prophets, who constantly warned that being God's people meant greater responsibility (Amos 3:2). Israel's calling was to be 'a light to those in darkness' (Isa 42:6-7); Paul says that when God's people break the covenant, 'the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles' (Isa 52:5; Ezek 36:20). The hope of a circumcised heart comes from Deuteronomy 30:6 and Jeremiah 31:33, promises for the time after exile. Paul is not attacking Judaism; he is using its own scriptures to say that the promised renewal has to happen from the inside.
13600: Jewish believers might feel stung: their privileges seem to count for less. Gentile believers might feel unexpectedly honoured: Gentiles who 'do by nature what the law requires' (2:14) are taken seriously. But the chapter also warns Gentiles who had begun to look down on Jews (11:18) that judging others is the very sin Paul just exposed.
13601: Romans 2 confronts religious insiders of every kind. Knowing the Bible, attending church or holding correct doctrine cannot replace a changed heart. It also insists that God's final judgment will take account of how people actually lived (2:6-7), a verse every tradition must reckon with.
13602: 'You repay each one according to his work' (also Prov 24:12), quoted in Rom 2:6.
13603: 'My name is continually blasphemed' because of Israel's exile; Paul cites it in Rom 2:24.
13604: God promises to circumcise his people's hearts after exile, the hope behind Rom 2:29.
13605: The new covenant writes the Law on the heart, echoed in Rom 2:15.
13606: Romans 2:6-13 is purely hypothetical: Paul describes salvation by works only to show it is impossible.
13607: This is genuinely debated. Some (Douglas Moo, for example) read it as stating the Law's standard, which no one in fact meets. Others (Wright, Thomas Schreiner, Simon Gathercole) think the Gentiles 'doing the law' are Christians transformed by the Spirit, and that final judgment according to works is real, though based on God's prior grace. Either way, Paul is not teaching salvation by merit.
13608: God Is Faithful; the Messiah Is the Answer
13609: Paul asks: then what advantage is there in being a Jew? Much: they were entrusted with God's words, and human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness. A chain of scripture shows that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin. Then comes the turning point: now God's righteousness has been revealed apart from the Law, through the faith(fulness) of Jesus the Messiah, whose death is the place of atonement, so that God is both just and the justifier. Boasting is excluded, because God is God of Jews and Gentiles alike.
13610: Paul's opponents accused him of teaching 'let us do evil that good may come' (3:8). His gospel of grace for the ungodly was controversial. Rom 3:21-26 is extremely compact, and some scholars think Paul is adapting an earlier Jewish-Christian confession about Jesus' death. It is the most debated paragraph in the letter.
13611: 'Redemption' (apolytrōsis) was the word for buying back a slave or prisoner. 'Justify' belongs to the lawcourt: a judge declares who is in the right. 'Boasting' was a feature of honour culture: people publicly claimed status. Paul says the Messiah's cross leaves no room for anyone, Jew or Gentile, to claim superior honour before God.
13612: The big question of 3:1-8 is God's own faithfulness (pistis) and righteousness: has God kept faith with Israel when Israel has not? Paul says yes. The word for atonement, hilastērion, is the Greek name for the 'mercy seat' where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). Jesus' death is presented as the place where God meets and deals with sin, publicly. The Shema ('the LORD is one', Deut 6:4) is used in 3:30: because God is one, he must be the God of all nations, so he justifies Jews and Gentiles on the same basis. Paul ends by saying faith 'establishes' the Law (3:31), not abolishes it.
13613: Jewish believers would welcome 3:1-4: Israel's privileges are real, and God is faithful. They would also hear their own psalms quoted to show that sin is universal. Gentile believers would hear that they stand on level ground with Jews, justified the same way. 'Is he not the God of Gentiles also?' was the sentence both groups needed to hear about each other.
13614: Rom 3:23 ('all have sinned') is usually quoted alone. In context, it explains why there is 'no distinction' between Jew and Gentile (3:22). The cross levels every group. This chapter also shows Paul caring as much about God being proved faithful and just as about humans being forgiven.
13615: David confesses his sin so that God is 'justified' in his words; quoted in Rom 3:4.
13616: 'There is none righteous': the first of a chain of psalms and prophets in Rom 3:10-18.
13617: 'No one living is righteous before you', echoed in Rom 3:20.
13618: The mercy seat on the Day of Atonement, the background to hilastērion in Rom 3:25.
13619: The Shema: God is one, so he is the God of Jews and Gentiles (Rom 3:29-30).
13620: Rom 3:23 is the start of a personal salvation plan: you are a sinner, so you need Jesus.
13621: True, but in Paul's argument the verse serves a larger point: since all have sinned, Jew and Gentile have equal access to God's grace in the Messiah, and neither can boast over the other (3:27-30).
13623: Paul turns to Abraham, the founding father. Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness' (Gen 15:6), and that happened before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father both of the uncircumcised who believe and of the circumcised who follow in his steps of faith. God's promise that he would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, by grace, so that it would be sure for all his offspring. Abraham's faith was trust in the God who gives life to the dead.
13624: Abraham was the central figure in Jewish debates about identity and righteousness. Some Jewish writings of the period presented Abraham as faithful in keeping God's commands even before Sinai (for example Sirach 44:19-21 and Jubilees). Paul enters this conversation and reads Abraham's story in the order Genesis tells it: promise and faith in Genesis 15, circumcision later in Genesis 17.
13625: 'Counted' (logizomai) is an accounting word: a sum entered in a ledger. Paul contrasts wages owed to a worker with a gift given freely (4:4-5), drawing on everyday experience of employment and patronage. Ancestry mattered enormously in honour culture; to call Abraham 'our forefather according to the flesh' and then say he is father of uncircumcised Gentiles was socially explosive.
13626: This chapter is about Abraham's family, the covenant question at the heart of Romans. God promised Abraham he would be 'father of many nations' (Gen 17:5) and that in him all nations would be blessed (Gen 12:3). Paul argues that this promise is fulfilled when Gentiles trust Israel's God and are counted as Abraham's children. David's Psalm 32 adds that God's blessing includes forgiving sins and not counting them. Abraham's faith in a God who 'gives life to the dead' (4:17) foreshadows faith in the God who raised Jesus.
13627: For Gentile believers, this chapter gave them a family tree: they were not second-class guests but Abraham's children. For Jewish believers, it honoured Abraham as their father too, but asked them to see the uncircumcised as brothers and sisters. Both were invited to imitate Abraham's hope against hope (4:18).
13628: Romans 4 shows that faith is not mere agreement with facts but trust in God's promise when circumstances say it is impossible. It also roots Christian identity in Israel's story: believers have a Jewish father in faith. Churches divided by ethnicity are reminded that God's promise was always for many nations.
13629: Abraham believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness: the text the whole chapter expounds.
13630: David's blessing on the one whose sin is forgiven and not counted, linked to Gen 15:6 by the shared word 'count'.
13631: 'Father of many nations': the promise Paul sees fulfilled in Gentile believers.
13632: Is anything too hard for the Lord? The background to Abraham's faith in the God who gives life to the dead.
13633: Abraham is simply an example of an individual saved by faith rather than works.
13634: He is that, but Paul's main concern is who belongs to Abraham's family. Abraham is 'the father of us all' (4:16), Jew and Gentile, because God's promise was always for many nations and always received by trust.
13635: Peace with God: Adam and the Messiah
13636: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God, access to grace and hope of sharing God's glory, even through suffering. God shows his love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies. Paul then compares Adam and Christ: through one man's disobedience sin and death entered the world and reigned; through one man's obedience grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life. The Law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace overflowed.
13637: Chapter 5 begins the second movement of the letter. Paul shifts from 'faith' language to 'life', 'hope', 'love' and 'Spirit'. The Roman church lived with real suffering: insecurity after the expulsion under Claudius, social suspicion of a strange new group, and the hardships of slaves and poor members.
13638: 'Peace' (pax) was Rome's great boast: the Pax Romana, celebrated on coins and in the Altar of Peace built for Augustus. It was peace imposed by conquest. Paul offers peace with God made by reconciliation, an enemy being won over. 'Access' (prosagōgē) could describe being introduced into a king's presence by a patron. Dying for a good person (a patron or benefactor) was imaginable; dying for an enemy was not (5:7-8).
13639: Jewish writings of the time (for example 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, written later in the first century) reflected on Adam's sin and its effects on humanity. Paul reads Israel's calling as God's answer to Adam: God called Abraham to undo Adam's ruin. But the Law, given to Israel, actually showed sin more clearly (5:20). Jesus, the faithful Israelite and true human, finally does what Adam and Israel failed to do. The 'love of God poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit' echoes the prophetic promise of the Spirit poured out (Joel 2:28).
